the figure for.n: The figure for is a phrase used to point to the number or statistic that belongs to one particular item, such as a country, year, group or product. It is common in reports, news and exam charts: the figure for 2020, the figure for women. The word corresponding often follows it when you compare two sets of data. It is more specific than just the number, because it implies an official or measured total. Pair it with was, rose, fell or stood at, and use the figure for X was higher than the figure for Y to compare.
x: The figure for unemployment last year was the lowest since 1990.
The figure for women is almost double the figure for men.
Officials have not yet published the figure for the final quarter.

reinforce.n: To reinforce something is to make it stronger or more firmly established, whether it is a belief, a habit, a message or a physical structure. Common objects are stereotypes, learning, behaviour, a point and walls or bridges. It is close to strengthen, but reinforce often means adding support to something that already exists, so it suits ideas that are repeated or confirmed. In teaching, repeated practice reinforces what was learned. The noun is reinforcement, and reinforced concrete contains steel bars.
x: Regular practice helps reinforce what students learn in class.
The new evidence reinforces the view that sleep affects memory.
Engineers reinforced the old bridge with steel beams.

terminate.n: To terminate something is to bring it to an end, usually by a decision or an official act rather than by letting it run out naturally. Typical objects are contracts, employment, agreements, pregnancies and computer processes. It sounds more official than end and is common in legal, business and technical writing. Terminate a contract and terminate employment are the most useful collocations. It can also be intransitive: the train terminates at this station. The noun is termination, and the adjective terminal.
x: The company may terminate the agreement with thirty days' notice.
Her employment was terminated after the department closed.
This bus route terminates at the central station.

compute.n: To compute is to work out an amount or number using mathematics or a machine. Typical objects are averages, totals, costs, rates and probabilities. It is close to calculate, but compute sounds more technical and is common in science, statistics and computing, where a computer computes a result. In everyday speech people say work out. If something does not compute, it makes no sense, which is an informal idiom. Related words are the noun computation and the adjective computational.
x: The software computes the monthly repayments automatically.
Researchers computed the risk for each age group separately.
It is easy to compute the area of a rectangle.

mutual.n: Mutual describes a feeling or action shared equally by two or more people or groups, so that each gives and receives the same thing. Common collocations are mutual respect, mutual benefit, mutual trust, mutual understanding and mutual agreement. It is close to reciprocal, but mutual is far more frequent in everyday English. A mutual friend is someone you and another person both know. Place it before a noun: a mutual decision. It is not normally used for something that only one side feels.
x: The two companies ended the partnership by mutual agreement.
Good teamwork depends on mutual trust and open communication.
We met through a mutual friend at a conference.

random.n: Random describes something that happens or is done without a plan, pattern or clear reason; in statistics it means every possibility has an equal chance of being chosen. In research you will meet a random sample and random selection; in daily life, a random act or a random question. The phrase at random means without any system. It is close to arbitrary, but random stresses chance, while arbitrary suggests a decision made without good reason. Informally, random can also describe something unexpected or odd. The noun is randomness.
x: Winners are chosen at random from all the entries.
The teacher asked a random student to read the answer aloud.
Participants were divided into two groups by random selection.

reluctance.n: Reluctance is the feeling of not wanting to do something, often because you are unsure, worried or embarrassed. It is usually followed by to plus a verb: reluctance to speak, reluctance to change. Typical patterns are show reluctance, overcome reluctance and with some reluctance. It is a little stronger than hesitation, which can be brief, and weaker than refusal, because the person may still agree in the end. The adjective is reluctant and the adverb is reluctantly.
x: Many men show a reluctance to talk about their health.
She agreed, but with obvious reluctance.
The manager's reluctance to delegate slowed the whole project.

tension.n: Tension has two main meanings: a nervous, anxious feeling, or a tense situation in which people or groups are close to conflict. Typical collocations are ethnic tension, political tension, growing tension, ease the tension and create tension. In a story, tension is the excitement that keeps you reading. Physically, it is also the tightness of a rope or muscle. It is milder than conflict, because it describes bad feeling before open fighting. Use between: tension between two countries.
x: There is growing tension between the two neighbouring countries.
A joke from the manager helped ease the tension in the room.
Stress often causes tension in the neck and shoulders.

cast doubt on.n: To cast doubt on something means to make it seem less certain, reliable or true. The subject is usually evidence, a study, a report or an event, and the object is a claim, result, theory or story: new evidence casts doubt on the official account. It is a fixed phrase, so keep doubt without an article. Add serious, considerable or fresh before doubt for emphasis. It is close to question and undermine, but it is more neutral: it does not prove something false. Common in news and academic writing.
x: Some experts say the discovery could cast doubt on the traditional theory of how the pyramids were built.
Several errors in the data cast doubt on the results.
Her sudden change of story cast doubt on everything she had said.

cosmos.n: The cosmos is the universe seen as one ordered, complete system, and the word usually carries a sense of vastness and wonder. It is used in science writing, philosophy and poetry: explore the cosmos, the origin of the cosmos. It is close to universe, but cosmos suggests order and harmony and sounds more literary. Space refers to the region beyond Earth. Use the before it, and treat it as uncountable. The adjective is cosmic, as in cosmic radiation, and cosmology is the study of the universe's origin.
x: Astronomers use powerful telescopes to study the early cosmos.
Ancient peoples believed that the cosmos was governed by the gods.
Looking at the stars, she felt very small in the vast cosmos.

doping.n: Doping is the use of banned drugs or substances by athletes to improve their performance in sport. It is an uncountable noun and appears in doping test, doping scandal, doping ban and doping control. It is narrower than cheating, since it refers specifically to drugs and sometimes to banned methods such as blood transfusions. The related verb is to dope, and an athlete who tests positive is said to have failed a drugs test. Use it in sports journalism and discussions of fairness.
x: The athlete received a four-year ban for doping.
Strict doping controls are carried out before every major race.
Many fans lost trust in the sport after the doping revelations.

endurance.n: Endurance is the ability to keep going through something difficult, tiring or painful for a long time, in body or in mind. It is an uncountable noun: physical endurance, mental endurance, a test of endurance, build up endurance. In sport, endurance events are long ones such as marathons and cycling races. It is close to stamina, which focuses on physical energy, while endurance can include patience in hard times. The verb is endure, and the adjective is enduring, meaning lasting.
x: Swimming across the lake required great strength and endurance.
Regular running will gradually build your endurance.
The long winter was a real test of the villagers' endurance.

famine.n: A famine is a period when a region or country has a severe shortage of food, so that many people suffer from hunger and some die. Typical collocations are widespread famine, severe famine, cause famine, famine relief and the Irish famine. It is stronger and more extreme than a food shortage, and it is used for large-scale disasters caused by drought, war or crop failure. It can be countable or uncountable. Do not confuse it with hunger, the feeling of needing food.
x: The government asked other countries for help as famine spread.
Failed harvests and civil war brought famine to the north.
Charities launched an appeal to raise money for famine relief.

nostalgic.n: Nostalgic describes the warm, slightly sad feeling you have when you remember happy times in the past, or something that causes that feeling. Use it with about, for or over: nostalgic about my school days, nostalgic for the 1990s. Other collocations are feel nostalgic, a nostalgic song and nostalgic memories. It is close to sentimental and wistful, but nostalgic always points to the past. The noun is nostalgia. It is usually gentle and positive, though it can sometimes suggest an unrealistic view of old times.
x: Walking through my old school made me feel nostalgic.
Many adults are nostalgic for the music of their teenage years.
The film is a nostalgic look at life in a small seaside town.

overtake.n: To overtake means to become greater in number, amount or importance than something else that was ahead before. Typical subjects are sales, companies, countries, cities and technologies: mobile phones overtook landlines. It is close to surpass and exceed, but overtake suggests a race in which one thing passes another. The same verb is used for vehicles, as in overtaking a lorry on the road. It is irregular: overtake, overtook, overtaken. The object is the thing that was previously ahead.
x: India is expected to overtake China as the most populous country.
Streaming has overtaken traditional television in many households.
Electric cars could overtake petrol models within a decade.

subsidy.n: A subsidy is money paid by a government or public body to reduce the cost of a product or service, or to help an industry or group. Typical collocations are government subsidy, farm subsidies, housing subsidy, fuel subsidy and receive or cut a subsidy. The plural is subsidies. It is different from a grant, which is usually a one-off payment for a project, while a subsidy keeps prices lower or supports ongoing activity. The verb is subsidise (subsidize in American English), and subsidised means partly paid for by the state.
x: The government pays a subsidy to companies that install solar panels.
Critics say a fuel subsidy encourages people to waste energy.
Students can get a subsidy towards the cost of public transport.

surge.n: A surge is a sudden, strong increase in the amount, number or level of something. It is followed by in: a surge in demand, a surge in prices, a surge in interest. Other collocations are sudden surge, a surge of anger and a power surge in electricity. It is more dramatic than a rise, because it suggests speed and force, like a wave. It is the opposite of a slump or sharp fall. As a verb, surge also means to move forward strongly, as crowds or water do.
x: Hospitals reported a surge in patients during the cold weather.
There was a sudden surge of interest in electric bikes.
A power surge damaged several computers in the office.

patron.n: A patron is a person who gives money or support to artists, writers, charities or other organisations, often over a long time. A patron of the arts is the classic collocation, and wealthy patron is also common. A patron can also be a regular customer of a shop, restaurant or library, which is a more formal use in the sense of customer. It is close to sponsor or benefactor, but patron often suggests personal support and influence. The related noun patronage means that support. A patron saint is a saint who protects a place or group.
x: The museum was founded by a generous patron of the arts.
The theatre thanked its patrons for their continued support.
Saint Patrick is the patron saint of Ireland.

penalty.n: A penalty is a punishment for breaking a law, rule or contract, such as a fine, a prison sentence or a loss of points. Typical collocations are heavy penalty, severe penalty, the death penalty, a penalty for late payment and impose a penalty. In football, a penalty is a free shot at goal after a foul in the penalty area, and a penalty shootout decides a drawn match. It is close to punishment, but penalty is more official and is often fixed in advance by a rule. Use for before the offence: a penalty for speeding.
x: There is a financial penalty for returning the books late.
The maximum penalty for this crime is ten years in prison.
The referee awarded a penalty after the defender fouled the striker.

pending.n: Pending describes something that is waiting to be decided, settled or completed. It appears before a noun, as in a pending application or a pending decision, or after a verb, as in the case is still pending. Typical collocations are pending approval, pending review and pending investigation. It can also act as a preposition meaning until or while waiting for: he was suspended pending an inquiry. It is close to awaiting and undecided, and on websites a pending payment is one not yet confirmed.
x: Your order is pending until the payment has been confirmed.
Two legal cases against the company are still pending.
The player was suspended pending the outcome of the investigation.
